subject: giant centipede
title: On One Island the Top Predator Is a Centipede. It Hunts Baby Birds

scenes.text: On one Pacific island, the top predator has no bones. And it hunts birds.
Phillip Island is a speck of land 870 miles east of Australia. At night, something crawls out of the leaf litter.
It's a centipede almost a foot long. It slips into seabird burrows and finds the chicks resting in the dark.
It strikes at the back of the neck and injects venom through a pair of pincer-like claws.
Scientists did the math in 2021. These centipedes take up to 3,700 petrel chicks every year.
And the island needs them. Every chick they eat moves nutrients from the ocean into the soil.

description:
On Phillip Island, in the Norfolk Island group of the South Pacific, the top predator is a centipede.
The Phillip Island centipede (Cormocephalus coynei) grows to almost 30 cm (about a foot). It hunts at night, and a 2021 study in The American Naturalist (Halpin and colleagues) estimated that the population kills between 2,109 and 3,724 black-winged petrel chicks a year, striking at the back of the neck and injecting venom through its forcipules. Vertebrates, including geckos, skinks and scavenged fish, make up about 48 percent of its diet, and seabird chicks about 8 percent. Because the petrels feed at sea, the centipedes end up carrying ocean nutrients onto the island, which helps its vegetation recover.
Would you sleep on that island? Comment below.
first_comment: Nearly half of this centipede's diet is animals with backbones: geckos, skinks, fish and chicks. Would you sleep on that island?
